content: Efforts should be made to raise awareness about tuberculosis (TB) and the severe social and economic consequences it can cause, particularly when the disease is not addressed early. Misconceptions about TB, as well as the stigma and discrimination faced by those affected, should be identified and actively countered. For patients who have been lost to follow-up during TB treatment, it is essential to notify healthcare staff immediately when a patient misses a treatment day. Efforts should be made to locate the patient, understand the reasons for missed treatment, and facilitate their return to treatment under the guidance of healthcare staff. It is important to confirm that all referred individuals are seen by the health service. Participation in community-based TB screening initiatives organized by health facilities or partner organizations is also encouraged. Providing health education and motivational support can help patients complete their treatment. Additional support, such as logistical or emotional assistance, should be offered to those undergoing preventive treatment. In settings where community-based care is provided, TB medications should be collected from the health facility by authorized personnel and stored appropriately. Accurate and timely recording of all patient visits is necessary, with submission of reports following established guidelines. Patient cards should be maintained meticulously. The collection, storage, and transport of biological specimens for TB testing require strict adherence to quality standards. The accuracy of laboratory tests depends on the quality of the specimens collected. Specimens should be checked for quality before processing, and accepted specimens must be recorded in the laboratory register. Proper organization of specimen transport is essential, and results should be accurately documented. Sputum collection should never occur in enclosed spaces such as laboratories, toilets, waiting areas, or reception rooms. Outdoor collection is preferred, as infectious droplets are quickly diluted, and ultraviolet light from the sun can inactivate TB bacteria. Alternatively, ventilated sputum collection rooms or booths may be used, provided they are properly ventilated and decontaminated. Visual aids such as posters and leaflets can be used to guide patients on sputum production. Specimens should be collected in sterile, disposable containers with tightly fitting screw caps to prevent leakage. Patients should be instructed to rinse their mouths with water before producing sputum to remove food particles. They should be guided to produce sputum from the lower airways and lungs through deep coughing. The collected specimen should be thick, mucoid, and may appear white-yellow or blood-tinged. Care must be taken to avoid contamination of the container or its lid. If a patient cannot spontaneously produce sputum, techniques such as deep breathing or aerosol inhalation may be used to induce coughing. After collection, the laboratory specimen requisition form should be completed. For urine-based TB tests, midstream urine should be collected in a fresh, standard container. Specimens should ideally be delivered to the laboratory and processed on the same day. If immediate delivery is not possible, specimens must be stored appropriately. Sputum specimens should be refrigerated at 2–8°C to prevent bacterial contamination. If refrigeration is unavailable, specimens can be stored in coolers with ice packs. Fresh urine specimens can be processed within eight hours at room temperature or refrigerated for up to three days. For longer delays, urine specimens should be frozen at -20°C or colder. Transport of specimens should occur as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours of collection. Specimens must be kept refrigerated and transported on ice. Triple packaging is required for safe transport of infectious materials, including an absorbent-wrapped container, secondary packaging (e.g., a sealed bag), and shock-resistant outer packaging. Local and international transport must comply with biosafety and regulatory requirements. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends standardized TB treatment regimens based on drug resistance profiles. These regimens are periodically reviewed and must be tailored to individual patients by TB specialists. For drug-susceptible TB, a 4-month all-oral treatment regimen is preferred due to its shorter duration, effectiveness, and reduced burden on patients and healthcare systems. For multidrug-resistant (MDR) or rifampicin-resistant (RR) TB, shorter all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline are recommended for eligible patients. Longer regimens are prescribed for those ineligible for shorter regimens, ensuring at least four effective drugs during the intensive phase and three during the continuation phase. Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB requires individualized treatment under specific conditions, including ethical approval and patient-centered care. Patient-centered TB care should address individual needs and preferences, ensuring convenient treatment options. Health education and counseling should support treatment adherence, with interventions tailored to patient needs and available resources. These may include direct communication, material support (e.g., food or transport fees), psychological support, and staff education. Treatment administration options include directly observed treatment (DOT) by trained providers, video-observed treatment (VOT), or unsupervised treatment, depending on feasibility and patient circumstances. Adverse drug effects should be closely monitored, with appropriate management based on the severity of symptoms. Minor effects, such as nausea or joint pain, may not require treatment interruption, while major effects, such as severe neuropathy or hepatitis, necessitate immediate medical attention. Treatment for latent drug-resistant TB infection should be carefully considered, focusing on high-risk household contacts and ensuring close monitoring for adverse events and progression to active disease.
